questions.stem: How does normal inspiration tend to assist systemic venous return?
options: It closes all systemic venous valves simultaneously.
It increases peripheral venous capacitance until return stops.
Lower chest pressure draws venous blood toward the heart.
It increases right atrial pressure and reduces abdominal pressure.
questions.why: Inspiration decreases intrathoracic pressure and promotes a pressure gradient drawing blood from peripheral veins to the thorax.

notes.A: Venous valves do not all close in inspiration.
notes.B: Return is generally supported rather than abolished.
notes.D: Lower rather than higher thoracic pressure assists inflow.

questions.stem: Arterial pressure inside an arteriole is unchanged, but pressure in its surrounding tissue rises. What happens to transmural pressure?
options: It increases because the pressure difference widens.
It decreases because the pressure difference narrows.
It becomes identical to intravascular arterial pressure.
It remains fixed because arterial pressure is unchanged.
questions.why: Transmural pressure equals internal pressure minus surrounding tissue pressure; increasing the latter reduces the difference.

notes.A: A higher external pressure reduces, rather than widens, the difference.
notes.C: It equals internal pressure only when external pressure is zero.
notes.D: Transmural pressure depends on both internal and external pressure.

questions.stem: Why does the fetal cardiovascular system divert much blood away from the pulmonary circuit before birth?
options: Pulmonary vascular resistance is exceptionally low before birth.
Pulmonary arterial pressure stays below placental venous pressure throughout fetal life.
The placenta oxygenates blood; fetal lungs resist flow.
Umbilical arteries carry already oxygenated blood to the heart.
questions.why: The placenta performs gas exchange before birth; fluid-filled fetal lungs have high resistance, favouring right-to-left shunts.

notes.A: Pulmonary resistance is high before aeration.
notes.B: The fetal left ventricle contributes significantly to systemic output.
notes.D: Umbilical arteries carry relatively deoxygenated blood toward placenta.

questions.stem: A patient develops cardiac tamponade. Why can stroke volume fall despite a normal blood volume?
options: High pericardial pressure restricts ventricular filling.
Tamponade increases functional ventricular compliance.
Tamponade directly raises venous return above normal.
The higher pericardial pressure directly increases end-diastolic ventricular volume.
questions.why: Elevated intrapericardial pressure limits end-diastolic filling and preload, reducing stroke volume. The restricted ventricular volume prevents an adequate Frank–Starling response.

notes.B: Tamponade reduces the ability of ventricles to expand.
notes.C: Venous return and effective filling become impaired.
notes.D: Valvular opening depends on pressure, but reduced preload is the central problem.

questions.stem: Heart rate rises from 70 to 80 beats/min while stroke volume stays at 70 mL. By how much does cardiac output increase?
options: By 1.40 litres per minute.
By 0.70 litres per minute.
By about 0.49 litres per minute.
By 0.80 litres per minute.
questions.why: The increase is 10 beats/min × 70 mL/beat = 700 mL/min, or 0.70 L/min.

notes.A: 1.40 L/min doubles the actual change.
notes.C: 0.49 L/min does not follow from the given rate change.
notes.D: 0.80 L/min treats the extra beats as a larger volume.

questions.stem: A burn patient presents with shock and an initially high haematocrit. What explains the contrast with recent whole-blood haemorrhage?
options: Burns cause immediate erythropoietin-driven erythrocytosis.
Plasma leakage leaves intravascular red cells concentrated.
Burns produce increased circulating volume despite shock.
Burns selectively destroy red cells circulating in blood.
questions.why: Severe burns can cause plasma to leak through damaged skin while red cells remain, producing haemoconcentration and raised haematocrit.

notes.A: Erythropoiesis is much too slow to explain this early result.
notes.C: Plasma loss reduces rather than increases effective circulating volume.
notes.D: Selective red-cell destruction would tend to lower red-cell concentration.

questions.stem: During graded exercise, which combination helps increase cardiac output?
options: Slower pacemaking and lower venous return.
Reduced sympathetic drive and greater afterload.
Higher rate, contractility and venous return.
Greater vagal activity and smaller stroke volume.
questions.why: Sympathetic drive raises heart rate and contractility while muscle pumping supports venous return, enabling higher cardiac output.

notes.A: Exercise generally increases rather than suppresses cardiac pumping.
notes.B: Reduced sympathetic drive does not explain exercise output.
notes.D: Vagal dominance would tend to slow the heart.

questions.stem: A patient has low circulating volume. Which hormone chiefly increases renal water retention and can constrict vessels at high concentration?
options: Endothelial prostacyclin.
Vasopressin, also called ADH.
Vasoactive intestinal peptide.
Atrial natriuretic peptide.
questions.why: ADH promotes renal water conservation and has a vasoconstrictor action when its level is high.

notes.A: Prostacyclin dilates vessels and limits platelet aggregation.
notes.C: VIP is a vasodilator rather than a water-retaining hormone.
notes.D: ANP promotes sodium and water loss.

questions.stem: How does local hypoxia affect most systemic arterioles versus pulmonary arterioles?
options: Both primarily constrict to lower oxygen delivery.
Both remain relatively insensitive to tissue oxygen.
Systemic vessels dilate; pulmonary vessels constrict.
Systemic vessels constrict while pulmonary vessels dilate.
questions.why: Systemic hypoxic tissues commonly dilate to improve supply, whereas low alveolar oxygen constricts adjacent pulmonary arterioles to improve ventilation–perfusion matching.

notes.A: Systemic tissues usually need increased flow in hypoxia.
notes.B: Oxygen tension influences both beds, but their dominant local responses differ.
notes.D: The response directions have been reversed.

questions.stem: After a meal containing long-chain fats, which pathway carries these lipids from the gut?
options: Renal filtration of absorbed fats.
Direct red-cell delivery to lacteals.
Oxygenated blood flow through the portal vein alone.
Chylomicron transport from intestinal lacteals.
questions.why: Absorbed long-chain fats are packaged into chylomicrons and enter lacteals, reaching the blood via lymphatic drainage.

notes.A: Kidneys do not mediate initial intestinal fat absorption.
notes.B: Red cells normally remain in blood vessels.
notes.C: Most long-chain dietary fat reaches systemic blood through lymph rather than directly through portal blood.

questions.stem: After three minutes upright, pressure changes from 126/82 to 104/77 mmHg. How is this classified using the chapter criterion?
options: No orthostatic hypotension because diastolic pressure fell only 5 mmHg.
Orthostatic hypotension only if both pressures fall by 20 mmHg.
Orthostatic hypotension because systolic pressure fell 22 mmHg.
No orthostatic hypotension because final systolic pressure exceeds 100 mmHg.
questions.why: A sustained systolic fall of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic fall of at least 10 mmHg within three minutes satisfies the criterion.

notes.A: The systolic threshold is met even when the diastolic threshold is not.
notes.B: The definition does not require both components to fall by 20 mmHg.
notes.D: The diagnostic threshold concerns the change, not a fixed final pressure.

questions.stem: Cardiac output falls by 20%, but total peripheral resistance rises by 25%. What happens to mean arterial pressure in the simplified MAP relation?
options: It decreases by approximately one quarter.
It increases by approximately one quarter.
It decreases by approximately one fifth.
It remains approximately unchanged.
questions.why: In MAP ≈ CO × TPR, 0.80 × 1.25 = 1.00, so the changes cancel mathematically.

notes.A: The combined product does not fall by one quarter.
notes.B: That ignores the fall in cardiac output.
notes.C: That ignores the compensatory rise in resistance.

questions.stem: Why might increasing heart rate far above normal eventually reduce cardiac output?
options: More beats per minute proportionally lengthen each ejection phase.
Diastolic time becomes longer and increases filling.
Systemic afterload falls enough to prevent forward ventricular ejection.
Shorter diastole reduces filling and stroke volume.
questions.why: Extreme tachycardia shortens diastole, reduces filling and may decrease stroke volume enough to lower output.

notes.A: Contractility does not necessarily become zero.
notes.B: Diastole shortens markedly at high rates.
notes.C: Normal valves do not remain permanently open during extreme tachycardia.

questions.stem: Why is a patient with significant coronary narrowing more vulnerable to angina when heart rate rises sharply?
options: The coronary sinus develops arterial hypertension.
The P wave disappears and blocks blood flow.
Shorter diastole and higher myocardial demand.
Myocardial oxygen consumption falls below baseline.
questions.why: Tachycardia increases cardiac oxygen demand and shortens diastole, reducing the time available for left ventricular coronary perfusion.

notes.A: The primary limitation is coronary supply through stenosed arteries during shortened diastole.
notes.B: An absent P wave is not the explanation of demand-related angina.
notes.D: Myocardial work and oxygen consumption generally rise with tachycardia.

questions.stem: A pressure tracing shows atrial contraction shortly after an ECG P wave and ventricular contraction shortly after QRS. What principle explains both delays?
options: The T wave must occur before either chamber can begin contraction.
Electrical excitation normally precedes the mechanical response of cardiac muscle.
Atrial and ventricular pressures directly create the corresponding ECG waves.
Mechanical contraction normally finishes before electrical activation begins in the chamber.
questions.why: The electrical depolarisation that activates cardiac muscle precedes its force development. P precedes atrial systole, and QRS precedes ventricular systole.

notes.A: The T wave reflects ventricular electrical recovery, after ventricular depolarisation.
notes.C: Pressure changes follow electrical activation and are not what skin ECG leads measure.
notes.D: This reverses the normal electrical-to-mechanical sequence.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects the updated interpretation of capillary fluid balance?
options: Interstitial oncotic forces remain independent of the endothelial glycocalyx.
Most capillaries continuously reabsorb nearly all filtered fluid at their venous ends.
The endothelial surface layer has little effect on filtration at rest.
The glycocalyx regulates filtration; lymph returns excess fluid.
questions.why: The revised Starling model includes the glycocalyx and emphasises that sustained net filtration is normally cleared by lymphatics.

notes.A: Protein distributions can influence effective oncotic gradients.
notes.B: The classical arterial filtration–venous reabsorption picture overstates sustained reabsorption.
notes.C: Lymphatic return remains vital even at normal pressures.

questions.stem: A patient with left-sided forward heart failure reports fatigue and produces very little urine. Which mechanism links the two?
options: Reduced systemic perfusion limits muscle and renal blood flow.
Elevated venous pressure increases renal filtration.
Pulmonary congestion causes systemic arteriolar dilation.
Increased left ventricular output stimulates renal water loss.
questions.why: Reduced blood ejected from the left heart impairs delivery to skeletal muscle and kidneys, causing fatigue and oliguria.

notes.B: Higher venous pressure does not directly improve GFR.
notes.C: The primary forward mechanism is reduced output, not pulmonary congestion.
notes.D: The syndrome involves reduced rather than excessive systemic delivery.

questions.stem: Once local metabolic dilation restores an organ’s blood flow, what prevents dilation from continuing unchecked?
options: The restored flow clears accumulated dilator metabolites.
The restored flow removes oxygen from the tissue cells.
The restored flow causes a sustained rise in local lactate.
The restored flow abolishes vessel-wall smooth muscle.
questions.why: The dilators exist because flow was too low for demand. Once flow matches demand, they are washed away as fast as they are made, so the arterioles regain their tone. This negative feedback stops dilation running away.

notes.B: Restored delivery generally improves tissue oxygen availability.
notes.C: Sustained lactate accumulation would favour continued dilation.
notes.D: Vascular smooth muscle remains present and functional.

questions.stem: A patient with marked polycythaemia has elevated haematocrit. What is the expected direct effect on systemic flow resistance?
options: Higher viscosity and lower resistance.
Lower viscosity and higher resistance.
Higher viscosity and higher resistance.
Lower viscosity and lower total vascular resistance.
questions.why: More red cells increase blood viscosity and consequently vascular resistance, raising the heart's workload.

notes.A: Higher viscosity raises resistance rather than lowering it.
notes.B: Lower viscosity does not follow from higher haematocrit.
notes.D: Both properties generally increase, not decrease.

questions.stem: The ST segment is nearly flat despite an actively contracting ventricle. What electrical state best explains that appearance?
options: The ventricle has completed repolarisation and returns to electrical rest.
The atria and ventricles are depolarising in opposite directions.
Most ventricular cells are depolarised together in their plateau phase.
The AV node is holding all impulses before ventricular activation.
questions.why: With much of the ventricular myocardium at a similar depolarised membrane potential during the plateau, there is little net voltage difference to register.

notes.A: Ventricular repolarisation occurs during the following T wave, not before ST.
notes.B: Atrial and ventricular opposing depolarisations do not account for normal ST isoelectricity.
notes.D: By ST, the impulse has already activated the ventricles.

questions.subtopic: QRS, ST, T and U waves

questions.stem: Which pressure relationship helps prevent fluid accumulation in normal pulmonary alveoli?
options: Absence of plasma proteins in pulmonary capillaries.
Higher alveolar protein pressure than in capillary plasma.
Pulmonary capillary pressure consistently exceeds systemic arterial pressure.
Relatively low pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure.
questions.why: Low pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure relative to plasma oncotic forces helps minimise filtration into air spaces.

notes.A: Plasma proteins contribute the inward oncotic force.
notes.B: Alveolar spaces normally contain little free fluid and protein.
notes.C: Pulmonary capillary pressure is much lower than systemic arterial pressure.

questions.stem: Increasing capillary hydrostatic pressure while other Starling forces stay unchanged tends to produce what?
options: Decreased outward fluid filtration.
More fluid filtration into tissues.
Increased plasma oncotic attraction.
Reversal of lymphatic flow.
questions.why: A higher capillary hydrostatic force favours filtration across the microvascular wall toward tissue. Raising venous pressure is one way to produce this hydrostatic change.

notes.A: The pressure favours outward, not reduced, filtration.
notes.C: Plasma oncotic pressure does not automatically increase.
notes.D: Lymphatic flow generally responds to excess tissue fluid rather than reversing.

questions.stem: Which contrast best distinguishes forward failure from backward failure?
options: Forward indicates excess cardiac output; backward low afterload.
Forward is confined to the right heart; backward to the left.
Forward is venous congestion; backward is low organ blood flow.
Forward reduces delivery; backward causes venous congestion.
questions.why: Forward failure describes inadequate delivery to downstream tissues, whereas backward failure describes elevated pressure and congestion upstream of a failing chamber.

notes.A: Reduced flow and congestion, not excessive output, are the defining patterns.
notes.B: Either side can produce both forward and backward consequences.
notes.C: The two effects are reversed in this statement.

questions.subtopic: Forward failure and low cardiac output

questions.stem: A region of heart muscle starts working harder. Which local product of its own metabolism helps increase its blood flow?
options: Adenosine formed as ATP is used up.
Noradrenaline from sympathetic nerves.
Angiotensin II formed in the blood.
Serotonin released by nearby platelets.
questions.why: Working muscle uses ATP faster, and its breakdown products (adenosine, ADP, AMP) build up and dilate the local arterioles. Flow rises in proportion to how hard the tissue works, which is why the heart relies so heavily on this.

notes.B: Noradrenaline is a nerve transmitter that mainly constricts arterioles via α₁ receptors.
notes.C: Angiotensin II is a circulating constrictor, not a product of the muscle’s metabolism.
notes.D: Platelet serotonin constricts vessels, and it comes from platelets, not from the working muscle.

questions.stem: Which pressure difference primarily drives blood back to the right atrium from the body?
options: Aortic systolic minus right ventricular systolic pressure.
Pulmonary venous minus pulmonary capillary pressure.
Left ventricular systolic minus aortic diastolic pressure.
Systemic filling pressure minus right atrial pressure.
questions.why: Venous return depends on the upstream systemic filling pressure relative to right atrial pressure and the resistance to venous return.

notes.A: Aortic-right ventricular systolic pressure is not the venous return driving gradient.
notes.B: Pulmonary venous pressure does not define systemic venous return.
notes.C: That difference is a pulse-pressure-related comparison.

questions.stem: A severely underperfused patient begins breathing rapidly, although the lungs were initially healthy. What drives this change?
options: Increased aerobic ATP production stimulates breathing.
Suppression of the peripheral chemoreceptors stimulates breathing.
Lactic acidosis stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors.
High tissue oxygen content increases respiratory drive.
questions.why: Inadequate tissue oxygen delivery promotes anaerobic metabolism and lactic acidosis. The resulting acidemia can stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors and increase ventilation; reduced oxygen delivery alone is not equivalent to low arterial oxygen tension.

notes.A: Aerobic metabolism is limited by inadequate oxygen delivery.
notes.B: Chemoreceptor stimulation, rather than suppression, promotes respiration.
notes.D: Excess oxygen is not the initiating problem in shock.

questions.stem: The CSF volume is about 150 mL and production is 550 mL/day. Approximately how many complete turnovers occur per day?
options: About 2.
About 1.
About 4.
About 6.
questions.why: Dividing daily production by total CSF volume gives 550/150 ≈ 3.7 turnovers each day.

notes.A: Two turnovers would require about 300 mL/day.
notes.B: One turnover would represent only about 150 mL/day.
notes.D: Six turnovers would correspond to around 900 mL/day.

questions.subtopic: CSF circulation, hydrocephalus and lumbar puncture

questions.stem: What does the mechanical stroke work of a ventricle represent?
options: Electrical energy in the SA node over one minute.
The number of coronary capillaries recruited.
Heart rate multiplied by body surface area.
Ventricular pressure–volume work per beat.
questions.why: The ventricle performs pressure–volume work as it ejects stroke volume against an arterial pressure load.

notes.A: Pacemaker electrical energy is not mechanical stroke work.
notes.B: Capillary recruitment affects supply, not the definition of work.
notes.C: Heart rate and surface area do not directly define mechanical work.

questions.stem: A technician places V1 at the fourth intercostal space. Where should the electrode be positioned horizontally?
options: At the anterior axillary line.
At the right sternal border.
At the left midaxillary line.
At the left midclavicular line.
questions.why: V1 is positioned in the fourth intercostal space at the right edge of the sternum; V2 lies at the left sternal edge at the same level.

notes.A: The anterior axillary position is used for V5.
notes.C: The midaxillary position is used for V6.
notes.D: The left midclavicular line in the fifth space is the usual site of V4.

questions.stem: A bleeding patient has a nearly normal arterial pressure but cold skin and reduced urine output. What is the best conclusion?
options: Normal pressure excludes significant shock.
Low perfusion can coexist with normal pressure.
Blood flow to all organs must remain normal.
Cardiac output must be above its pre-bleeding level.
questions.why: Sympathetic arteriolar constriction can maintain arterial pressure despite reduced cardiac output and poor perfusion of some tissues.

notes.A: Shock is defined by inadequate tissue perfusion, not one pressure value.
notes.C: Flow can be redistributed away from skin and kidneys.
notes.D: Haemorrhage reduces venous return and usually lowers output.

questions.stem: Why may advanced liver disease cause generalised oedema even without venous obstruction?
options: Less albumin synthesis reduces plasma oncotic pressure.
Liver failure directly shuts every lymphatic valve.
Excess albumin synthesis draws water into tissues.
A rise in plasma protein concentration stops absorption.
questions.why: Reduced albumin production lowers intravascular colloid oncotic pressure, allowing more net filtration and oedema.

notes.B: Lymphatic valve closure is not the universal mechanism.
notes.C: Advanced liver disease commonly reduces albumin synthesis.
notes.D: Plasma protein concentration is decreased, not increased.

questions.stem: At one instant, Lead I records +0.4 mV and Lead III records −0.2 mV. What must Lead II record?
options: −0.2 mV, from using the third lead alone.
+0.6 mV, from adding their magnitudes.
−0.6 mV, from subtracting the two values.
+0.2 mV, from adding the signed voltages.
questions.why: Einthoven’s law is V(II) = V(I) + V(III). Therefore +0.4 + (−0.2) = +0.2 mV at the same instant.

notes.A: Lead II is obtained by combining the two measured limb-lead voltages.
notes.B: The negative sign of Lead III must be retained in the sum.
notes.C: This reverses the sign of the result rather than adding the signed voltages.

questions.stem: An exercising leg receives increased blood flow while its muscle continues contracting. What is this response called?
options: Active hyperaemia driven by ongoing tissue metabolism.
Autoregulation that holds its flow at rest level.
Baroreflex vasodilation after systemic arterial pressure rises.
Reactive hyperaemia following a temporary flow block.
questions.why: Active hyperaemia is the rise in flow while a tissue is working: its metabolites dilate the arterioles for as long as activity continues. Reactive hyperaemia is the surge after a blockage is released.

notes.B: The flow rises above baseline rather than staying constant.
notes.C: The increase originates largely from local demand, not a pressure-rise baroreflex.
notes.D: Reactive hyperaemia is a surge after an obstruction ends.

questions.stem: A harsh systolic murmur develops during blood ejection through a narrowed aortic valve. What mechanism explains it?
options: Opening of the aortic valve during ventricular relaxation.
Laminar blood flow through a normal-sized valve.
Regurgitation through the mitral valve during diastole.
Turbulent forward flow through a stenotic outflow orifice.
questions.why: Aortic stenosis accelerates blood through a narrow outlet during systole, causing a turbulent ejection murmur.

notes.A: The aortic valve opens when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure in systole.
notes.B: Laminar flow through normal valves ordinarily produces no such murmur.
notes.C: Mitral regurgitation usually occurs during systole, not diastole.

questions.stem: A highly active cortical region accumulates carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions. What is the expected local vascular response?
options: Local arterioles dilate, increasing perfusion.
Venules constrict without an arteriolar response.
Local arterioles constrict, reducing perfusion.
Capillaries close while arteriolar tone stays fixed.
questions.why: Increased local CO₂ and H⁺ cause cerebral arteriolar vasodilation, improving blood delivery to metabolically active tissue.

notes.B: Isolated venular constriction does not explain metabolic regulation of cerebral arteriolar inflow.
notes.C: Constriction would reduce flow to the region that needs more oxygen.
notes.D: Capillary closure would worsen rather than correct the local supply-demand mismatch.

questions.stem: Lead II has an upright QRS while aVR has a downward QRS during the same beat. What best explains the difference?
options: Atrial and ventricular activity alternate between the leads on each beat.
One lead measures depolarisation and the other repolarisation.
Each lead projects the same electrical vector onto a different axis.
The two leads record different mechanical contractions.
questions.why: A lead is a directional electrical view. The normal mean ventricular depolarisation vector points generally towards Lead II and away from aVR.

notes.A: Lead orientation does not change the sequence of atrial and ventricular activation.
notes.B: Both QRS complexes represent ventricular depolarisation, despite opposite polarity.
notes.D: Both leads sample the electrical activity of the same heartbeat.

questions.stem: In a normal cardiac cycle, how does the rate of ventricular ejection change after the semilunar valves open?
options: Ejection peaks only after ventricular pressure has begun to fall.
It starts rapidly and then becomes reduced ejection.
It remains identical in flow throughout systole.
It starts slowly and accelerates until valve closure.
questions.why: The ejection phase has an initial rapid phase followed by reduced ejection as the pressure and flow relationship changes.

notes.A: Ejection occurs during ventricular systole, before relaxation.
notes.C: Ejection rate declines rather than remaining uniform.
notes.D: The pattern is the reverse of the usual ejection phases.

questions.stem: Minutes after a severe allergic exposure, a patient's pressure drops with generalised swelling. Which vascular action is most relevant?
options: Generalised constriction with reduced capillary permeability.
Histamine-related dilatation with increased capillary permeability.
Selective haemorrhage into the gastrointestinal tract.
Increased myocardial pump function with reduced venous capacitance.
questions.why: Anaphylaxis releases mediators including histamine that widen vessels and increase capillary leakage, reducing effective perfusion.

notes.A: Anaphylaxis typically causes dilation and increased leak.
notes.C: Occult bleeding is not the primary allergic vascular mechanism.
notes.D: Higher pump performance would not explain the sudden widespread leakage.

questions.stem: Why can chronic widespread alveolar hypoxia lead to pulmonary hypertension?
options: Persistent hypoxic constriction increases lung resistance.
Persistent hypoxia opens every pulmonary capillary without resistance.
Widespread hypoxia lowers pulmonary vascular smooth-muscle tone.
Chronic hypoxia eliminates blood passing through the lungs.
questions.why: When hypoxic constriction affects much of the lung, cumulative resistance rises and pulmonary arterial pressure can increase.

notes.B: Recruitment is a different response that lowers resistance.
notes.C: The lecture explicitly associates hypoxia with pulmonary vasoconstriction.
notes.D: Lung flow generally continues but faces increased resistance.

questions.stem: The jugular venous 'c' wave is chiefly linked to which event?
options: Right atrial contraction immediately before QRS.
Systolic bulging of the tricuspid valve.
Passive systemic venous filling late in systole.
Rapid emptying of the right atrium.
questions.why: Early right ventricular contraction can bulge the shut tricuspid valve toward the right atrium, contributing to the c wave.

notes.A: Right atrial systole generates the a wave.
notes.C: Venous filling behind a closed tricuspid valve makes the v wave.
notes.D: Rapid atrial emptying contributes to the y descent.

questions.stem: An isolated SA node fires at about 100 beats/min, whereas the same person’s resting pulse was about 70. Which interpretation best fits?
options: Resting sympathetic activity had restrained SA nodal firing.
Atrial conduction had slowed the spontaneous SA nodal rate.
Resting vagal activity had restrained SA nodal firing.
The cardiac pacemaker was intrinsically limited to 70.
questions.why: With no nerve input the SA node fires at about 100 beats/min. At rest the vagus releases acetylcholine continuously (vagal tone), holding the rate down to about 60–80. Blocking the vagus, for example with atropine, lets the rate rise.

notes.A: Sympathetic activity usually increases SA nodal firing.
notes.B: Atrial conduction is not the main cause of the slower intrinsic SA pacemaker rate.
notes.D: The isolated rate shows the pacemaker is capable of firing faster.

questions.stem: A patient with massive haemorrhage remains severely hypotensive after blood volume is completely restored. Which stage fits?
options: Postural hypotension from remaining upright.
Early compensated hypovolaemic shock with intact reflexes.
Transient vasovagal faint without major tissue damage.
Irreversible shock after extensive tissue injury.
questions.why: Severe myocardial, neural and microvascular damage may prevent recovery even after the original blood-volume loss has been corrected.

notes.A: Postural hypotension should depend on standing and impaired compensation.
notes.B: Compensated shock should retain useful mechanisms for pressure support.
notes.C: An uncomplicated faint generally improves rapidly when lying flat.

questions.stem: At an otherwise unchanged capillary, how would increased interstitial protein concentration affect fluid movement?
options: It strengthens plasma oncotic pressure, reducing filtration.
It increases protein attraction into the blood compartment.
It lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure, opposing filtration.
It strengthens the outward oncotic force favouring filtration.
questions.why: More interstitial protein increases interstitial colloid osmotic pressure, tending to pull fluid outward from the capillary and increase filtration.

notes.A: Plasma protein concentration is held constant; the changed force is interstitial.
notes.B: Increased proteins outside the capillary attract rather than remove interstitial water.
notes.C: A change in interstitial protein does not directly lower capillary pressure.

questions.stem: Regular P waves continue at one rate and QRS complexes at a slower independent rate, with no fixed PR relationship. Which rhythm disturbance is present?
options: Third-degree atrioventricular block.
Sinus rhythm with a normal PR interval.
First-degree atrioventricular block.
Second-degree atrioventricular block.
questions.why: Complete (third-degree) block produces atrioventricular dissociation: atria and ventricles follow independent rhythms without consistent P-to-QRS conduction.

notes.B: Normal sinus rhythm has a consistent P wave preceding each conducted QRS.
notes.C: First-degree block maintains a consistent P-to-QRS relationship with prolonged PR.
notes.D: Second-degree block has intermittent failure, rather than complete independence.

questions.stem: Two cylindrical vessels have equal transmural pressure, but vessel X has twice the radius of vessel Y. How do their required wall tensions compare?
options: Vessel X requires four times the tension of Y.
Both vessels require exactly the same wall tension.
Vessel X requires twice the wall tension of Y.
Vessel X requires half the wall tension of Y.
questions.why: For a cylinder, wall tension T = P × r. With equal transmural pressure, the vessel with twice the radius needs twice the tension. This is why a capillary’s tiny radius lets a one-cell wall withstand blood pressure.

notes.A: A fourfold difference does not follow the linear radius relation.
notes.B: Equal pressure alone does not make tension equal.
notes.D: Half the tension would apply to half the radius.

questions.stem: What physiological purpose is served by slow conduction through the AV node?
options: It allows atrial contraction to finish ventricular filling.
It prevents the impulse from ever reaching the ventricular myocardium.
It ensures ventricles eject before the atria contract.
It allows the aortic valve to remain open during atrial systole.
questions.why: The AV delay separates atrial and ventricular activation so atrial systole can augment ventricular filling before ventricular systole.

notes.B: Normal impulses subsequently travel through His and Purkinje fibres.
notes.C: The sequence is atrial activation before ventricular activation.
notes.D: The aortic valve remains closed during ordinary atrial systole.

questions.subtopic: AV nodal delay and heart block

questions.stem: A patient in compensated haemorrhagic shock has cold, pale skin. Which mechanism accounts for this?
options: Increased sympathetic cutaneous vasoconstriction.
Loss of vasomotor drive causing widespread dilation.
Increased skin capillary blood volume from vasodilation.
Direct activation of warm-sensitive skin receptors.
questions.why: Sympathetic constriction reduces skin flow to preserve perfusion for vital organs, producing pallor and coolness.

notes.B: Loss of sympathetic tone would usually warm and flush skin.
notes.C: Higher cutaneous blood volume tends to increase redness.
notes.D: The primary response is systemic compensation, not skin warming.

questions.stem: A graph of organ flow against perfusion pressure is almost flat over a middle range but slopes downward at very low pressures. Why?
options: The veins become the principal resistance at low pressure.
The arterioles reach their maximal dilation at low pressure.
The heart stops driving any pressure into the organ.
The arterioles reach their maximal constriction at low pressure.
questions.why: Once arterioles are fully dilated, they cannot reduce resistance further, so flow decreases as pressure falls.

notes.A: Venous vessels do not replace arterioles as the chief resistance site.
notes.C: A downward slope does not mean perfusion pressure is zero.
notes.D: Maximal constriction occurs in response to rising pressure, not very low pressure.

questions.stem: A ventricular action potential has a prolonged plateau. Which membrane currents chiefly sustain it?
options: Absence of calcium entry with continued chloride influx.
Calcium inflow balanced by outward potassium current.
Rapid sodium entry alone throughout the entire plateau.
Increased potassium efflux without any inward current.
questions.why: Slow inward calcium current and outward potassium current maintain the prolonged plateau before repolarisation.

notes.A: Calcium entry contributes substantially to phase 2.
notes.C: Fast sodium influx creates phase 0, not the sustained plateau.
notes.D: Unopposed potassium efflux would favour repolarisation.

questions.stem: During progressive shock, capillary hydrostatic pressure paradoxically rises while systemic arterial pressure is falling. Which microvascular pattern best explains it?
options: Open capillary entry with constricted venules.
Increased venular drainage with reduced capillary entry.
Precapillary constriction with freely draining venules.
Precapillary constriction with widened venous outlets.
questions.why: With capillary entry relatively open but venular outflow restricted, blood stagnates and local capillary pressure rises, driving fluid into the interstitium.

notes.B: Greater drainage would reduce rather than increase local stagnation.
notes.C: Lower entry with free outflow would not cause the described stasis.
notes.D: Both reduced entry and improved drainage favour lower capillary pressure.

questions.stem: During severe hepatic hypoperfusion, cells near the central vein are especially vulnerable to hypoxia. Why?
options: They are closest to arterial inflow.
They are located outside the hepatic sinusoidal network.
They receive blood with the highest oxygen content.
They are farthest downstream from the portal triads.
questions.why: Centrilobular cells receive blood after it has travelled from portal triads, making them less oxygenated and vulnerable.

notes.A: Oxygenated hepatic arterial inflow enters near the portal triads.
notes.B: Centrilobular hepatocytes remain within the sinusoidal perfusion system.
notes.C: Blood oxygen content generally falls as it traverses sinusoids.

questions.stem: How does calcium entering through L-type channels activate a much larger ventricular calcium signal?
options: It triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
It closes ryanodine receptors in the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
It causes SERCA to release its stored calcium outward.
It directly hydrolyses ATP within actin.
questions.why: Trigger calcium opens ryanodine receptors, releasing stored calcium in calcium-induced calcium release. This amplifies the small trigger signal into a large intracellular calcium release.

notes.B: Ryanodine receptors open rather than close in this mechanism.
notes.C: SERCA pumps calcium back into the SR during relaxation.
notes.D: Calcium binds troponin C; ATP hydrolysis occurs in cross-bridge cycling.

questions.stem: What extra perspective do the chest leads V1–V6 add to the standard limb-lead views?
options: They replace voltage measurement with intracardiac pressure.
They isolate atrial electrical activity from ventricular activity.
They remove the need to record the frontal electrical plane.
They show cardiac electrical vectors in the horizontal plane.
questions.why: The limb leads provide frontal-plane views, while the precordial leads examine the same heart from different points around the horizontal plane.

notes.A: Chest leads, like limb leads, still record surface electrical potentials.
notes.B: Both sets of leads record combined cardiac electrical events.
notes.C: Frontal and horizontal views complement rather than replace one another.

questions.stem: A haemorrhage suddenly lowers blood pressure. Which changes help restore it through the arterial baroreflex?
options: Increased vagal drive and reduced venous return.
Reduced sympathetic drive and increased vagal drive.
Increased sympathetic drive and reduced vagal drive.
Reduced sympathetic drive and greater venous storage.
questions.why: Lower afferent firing releases the pressor area and reduces vagal inhibition, raising heart rate, contractility and vascular tone.

notes.A: Greater vagal drive would slow the heart, while low return worsens output.
notes.B: That combination is appropriate to a rise in pressure.
notes.D: Sympathetic withdrawal and venous storage would further lower pressure.

questions.stem: For steady laminar flow through a straight tube, where is linear velocity highest?
options: At the endothelial wall.
At the vessel centre.
Uniformly across the lumen.
At the outer plasma layer.
questions.why: Viscous drag slows flow near the wall; a parabolic velocity profile has its greatest velocity near the centre.

notes.A: The no-slip boundary makes velocity near the wall approach zero.
notes.C: Laminar flow has a radial velocity gradient.
notes.D: The plasma layer adjacent to the wall is not the maximum-velocity region.

questions.stem: An ECG is repeated at 50 mm/s instead of 25 mm/s, with no change in the patient's conduction. How does the same 0.16-s PR interval appear?
options: It occupies twice the former number of horizontal squares.
It occupies the same number of horizontal squares.
It occupies half as many horizontal squares as on the slower recording.
It occupies twice the former number of vertical squares.
questions.why: Doubling paper speed doubles the horizontal distance covered during a fixed physiological interval. A 0.16-s PR interval spans 8 mm at 50 mm/s versus 4 mm at 25 mm/s.

notes.B: The number of squares changes because time calibration depends on paper speed.
notes.C: A faster recording speed spreads the same time over more paper, not less.
notes.D: Vertical squares measure voltage and are unaffected by horizontal paper speed.

questions.stem: An examination reveals raised JVP, a tender enlarged liver, ascites and ankle oedema. Which haemodynamic change unifies these?
options: High systemic venous pressure behind the right ventricle.
Increased pulmonary venous pressure without systemic congestion.
Reduced filtration from peripheral capillaries.
Reduced central venous pressure from depleted blood volume.
questions.why: Right ventricular backward failure elevates right atrial and systemic venous pressures, causing jugular distension, hepatic congestion and dependent oedema.

notes.B: Isolated pulmonary venous congestion principally reflects left-sided failure.
notes.C: Higher systemic venous pressure promotes, rather than reduces, filtration.
notes.D: Right-sided backward failure increases rather than decreases venous pressure.

questions.stem: What produces an S4 in a patient with a stiff ventricle?
options: Turbulence during systolic outflow across a normal aortic valve.
Opening of the pulmonary valve against high pressure.
Atrial contraction into a poorly compliant ventricle.
Rapid early-diastolic filling before any atrial activity.
questions.why: S4 is associated with late-diastolic atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, which causes low-frequency vibrations.

notes.A: Systolic ejection turbulence describes a murmur, not S4.
notes.B: Pulmonary valve opening occurs in systole.
notes.D: Rapid passive filling is associated with S3 rather than S4.

questions.stem: Brain glucose uptake remains adequate despite an intact blood-brain barrier that restricts passage between endothelial cells. What transport process explains this?
options: Through insulin-triggered endothelial pores.
Through a specific endothelial transporter.
By free movement through tight junctions.
Through bulk passage of plasma proteins.
questions.why: Glucose crosses the BBB through transporters such as GLUT1; its entry does not require insulin.

notes.A: Cerebral glucose transport is largely insulin independent.
notes.C: Endothelial tight junctions block most paracellular solutes.
notes.D: Protein leakage is limited by the barrier.

questions.stem: A cuff that is far too small is used on a large upper arm. Which measurement error is likely?
options: The cuff underestimates systolic pressure but overestimates diastolic pressure.
No systematic effect on cuff pressure.
Falsely low BP from excessive arterial unloading.
An undersized cuff gives a falsely high reading.
questions.why: An undersized cuff transmits pressure poorly around a large arm and commonly overestimates measured pressure.

notes.A: Both systolic and diastolic measurements may be distorted.
notes.B: Cuff size materially affects readings.
notes.C: A small cuff usually overestimates rather than underestimates BP.
